newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Grim data from Seoul underlines Pyongyang's crisis.
newsitem.headline: Grim data from Seoul underlines Pyongyang's crisis.

text.p: Crippled by shortages of energy and raw materials, North Korea's economy shrank for the seventh year in a row in 1996, South Korea's central bank said on Wednesday.
The report backed up growing evidence of impending catastrophe in North Korea, including film footage of skeletal toddlers and reports that 800,000 children were malnourished.
It also underlined a dilemma facing Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il as he prepares to formally take the reins of power in a nation with a broken economy and on the brink of famine.
To save the economy, and prevent millions of people starving to death, North Korea must open up, analysts agree. Yet any loosening of Stalinist controls may threaten the survival of the regime.
The country's gross domestic product fell a real 3.7 percent last year following a 4.6 percent decline in 1995, the Bank of Korea said in a report.
Manufacturing and construction output was down 8.9 percent and 11.8 percent respectively. Farm, forestry and fishery production was up one percent.

"Production in manufacturing and most other industrial sectors fell sharply due to the short supply of energy and raw materials and transport problems resulting from a delayed recovery from floods," the report said.
Foreign trade tracked industry's decline. In 1996, exports were estimated to have fallen to $730 million from $740 million in 1995 and imports to $1.25 billion from $1.31 billion.
Per-capita gross national product (GNP) dropped to $910 in 1996 from $957 in 1995.

By contrast, South Korea's per-capita GNP last year expanded to $10,548, almost 12 times the size of the North's, while its overall economic output of $452 billion was 22 times larger, the bank figures showed.
Since the secretive Stalinist nation does not release economic statistics, the central bank's data is largely based on educated guess-work.

Pyongyang announced on Tuesday the end of a three-year mourning period for Kim's father, "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, paving the way for the son to take over the vacant posts of state president and general secretary of the all-powerful Workers' Party.
But while Kim junior has been groomed for decades to step into his father's shoes, analysts say he is in no hurry to take charge in a desperate crisis.

On Tuesday, the Rome-based World Food Programme (WFP) released dramatic film footage of North Korea's food crisis, and said it would appeal on Wednesday for 129,000 tonnes of food worth $45.7 million for infants aged under six. One shot showed a five-year-old boy close to death on a hospital bed. Another revealed a girl, aged three, weighing just 10 kg (22 lb) and with skin sores. Other children had bowed legs, swollen joints and protruding stomachs.
The U.N. Children's Fund said 800,000 children aged under five were malnourished -- 37 percent of that age group.
A Seoul foreign ministry spokesman said South Korea would "seriously consider" the new U.N. appeal.

Meanwhile, a South Korean official said ceremonies on Tuesday in Pyongyang marking the end of official mourning for Kim Il-sung were notable because they concentrated on "the opening of Kim Jong-il's era".

Sin Eon-sang, a senior North Korea-watcher at the unification ministry, said the North Korean media described Kim Il-sung as the leader of the previous generation, and Kim Jong-il as the torchbearer for the new generation.
He said a hierarchy list released late on Tuesday contained no surprises.
